title: Where Crest Cells May Not Go

scenes.tts: Look along the spinal cord of a chick embryo. The sensory clusters called dorsal root ganglia sit in a neat, repeating row. No central planner lays them out. Their cells come from the neural crest, a population at the top of the neural tube. So what turns a crowd of wandering cells into a row?
scenes.visual: Neural tube on top, crest cells along its top edge, a row of ganglia below, question marks between them.
scenes.narration: Look along the spinal cord of a chick embryo. The sensory clusters called dorsal root ganglia sit in a neat, repeating row. No central planner lays them out. Their cells come from the neural crest, a population at the top of the neural tube. So what turns a crowd of wandering cells into a row?

scenes.tts: Crest cells begin as part of the tube's top edge. They loosen their grip on their neighbours. Then they crawl away. That change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is called an epithelial to mesenchymal transition. Biologists shorten it to E M T.
scenes.visual: A sheet of cells; the crest cell loosens, rounds up and crawls out.
scenes.caption: Crest cells begin as part of the tube's top edge. They loosen their grip on their neighbours. Then they crawl away. That change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is called an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Biologists shorten it to EMT.
scenes.narration: Crest cells begin as part of the tube's top edge. They loosen their grip on their neighbours. Then they crawl away. That change, from a cell in a sheet to a free cell, is called an epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition. Biologists shorten it to EMT.

scenes.tts: In the chick trunk, one route, called ventromedial, runs through the somites. Somites are the blocks of tissue beside the tube. The part of each block that will form vertebrae is the sclerotome. It has a front half, called rostral, and a back half, called caudal. Crest cells pass only through the rostral half.
scenes.visual: Tube above a row of somite blocks; each block split into rostral and caudal halves; crest cells stream into rostral halves only.
scenes.narration: In the chick trunk, one route, called ventromedial, runs through the somites. Somites are the blocks of tissue beside the tube. The part of each block that will form vertebrae is the sclerotome. It has a front half, called rostral, and a back half, called caudal. Crest cells pass only through the rostral half.

scenes.tts: The caudal half keeps them out. Crest cells carry a receptor called Eph B. Cells of the caudal half carry a signal on their surface, called ephrin B. Because it sits in the membrane, it works only when cells touch. When a crest cell touches ephrin B, the signal into the crest cell repels it, and it is pushed away.
scenes.visual: Close-up of one boundary: crest cell with receptor tabs meets the red caudal wall with ephrin tabs and is pushed back.
scenes.caption: The caudal half keeps them out. Crest cells carry a receptor called EphB. Cells of the caudal half carry a signal on their surface, called ephrin-B. Because it sits in the membrane, it works only when cells touch. When a crest cell touches ephrin-B, the signal into the crest cell repels it, and it is pushed away.
scenes.narration: The caudal half keeps them out. Crest cells carry a receptor called EphB. Cells of the caudal half carry a signal on their surface, called ephrin-B. scenes.tts: Researchers tested this in a dish. They laid alternating stripes of ephrin B and a control protein, and plated trunk crest cells on them. The cells avoided the ephrin B stripes. A sceptic could say the stripe is just a poor surface. So they added soluble ephrin B to the medium, meaning free in the liquid. That blocked the avoidance. The avoidance needs Eph and ephrin signaling.
scenes.visual: Striped dish; cells gather on control stripes; then soluble ephrin dots fill the dish and cells spread over all stripes.
scenes.caption: Researchers tested this in a dish. They laid alternating stripes of ephrin-B and a control protein, and plated trunk crest cells on them. The cells avoided the ephrin-B stripes. A sceptic could say the stripe is just a poor surface. So they added soluble ephrin-B to the medium, meaning free in the liquid. That blocked the avoidance. The avoidance needs Eph and ephrin signaling.

scenes.tts: Back in the embryo, the same rule applies. Crest cells enter the rostral half of each sclerotome and not the caudal half. That is why the dorsal root ganglia are segmented. Cells are not only drawn toward their targets. Where crest cells may not go helps shape what they build.
scenes.visual: Embryo stage again: cells enter rostral halves, are turned back at caudal halves, and gather into a row of ganglia.
